0.definition: A patch lies closer to end A when both its true-color and false-color halves are predominantly near-black, with faint contrast and few discernible surface features. End B has brighter, varied colors and recognizable landscape structure.
cues: Near-black coverage across both halves is much greater toward A.
Fields, roads, buildings, and vegetation boundaries are readily discernible toward B.
False-color vegetation appears strongly red toward B but is barely visible toward A.
Local color and brightness variation are much weaker toward A.

1.definition: A patch lies closer to A when broad, smooth areas of cropland, bare ground or sparse vegetation dominate, with relatively little tree canopy. It lies closer to B when dense, textured tree cover dominates, with open ground mostly confined to clearings or narrow strips.
cues: Dominant cover: extensive open surfaces in A versus largely continuous tree canopy in B.
Texture: smooth field interiors in A versus finely mottled or grainy canopy, sometimes arranged in rows, in B.
Color: A mixes pale tan ground and green or bright-red fields; B is predominantly dark green in true color and deeper red in false color.
Layout: A has broad exposed parcels with isolated trees or thin tree lines; B has clearings embedded within wooded blocks.

2.definition: A patch lies closer to A when more of its land shows exposed tan or brown ground and less shows bright white or cyan snow cover. Patches closer to B have extensive snow interspersed with dark vegetation and terrain features.
cues: B has extensive bright white to icy cyan areas in both composites; A largely lacks these.
A has broad tan or brown ground surfaces in true color, turning greenish or turquoise in false color.
B shows dark trees and wooded slopes contrasting sharply with bright snow; A shows trees against exposed earth.

3.definition: A patch lies closer to A when it shows more ridges, branching hollows, dark slope shadows and coarse, irregular land-cover patches, with fewer broad, smooth agricultural parcels. B is dominated by open green fields with clear boundaries and relatively little visible relief.
cues: Ridges and shadowed hollows in A versus comparatively smooth terrain in B.
Irregular, coarse-textured cover in A versus broad, clearly bounded field mosaics in B.
Mostly muted or dark near-infrared reds in A versus extensive bright red fields in B.
Roads and clearings winding around terrain in A versus field-aligned lanes and hedgerows in B.

4.definition: A patch lies closer to A when fine ridges, ripples, or mottled relief form a continuous texture across most of its area. It lies closer to B when broad, relatively uniform water surrounds distinct islands or borders a localized coastline. Judge spatial texture rather than overall brightness or color.
cues: A has repeated light–dark variations throughout the patch; B has large nearly uniform areas.
A’s water shows conspicuous elongated, often diagonal ripple bands.
B’s strongest contrasts outline isolated islands, rocks, or a coastal margin.
A’s land examples also show extensive irregular ridge-and-hollow texture.

5.definition: A patch lies closer to A when less of its land surface is covered by bright white to cyan snow and more exposed vegetation or brown ground is visible. B has extensive snow cover, often interrupted by dark wooded slopes.
cues: B has widespread bright white areas in true color that remain white or cyan in false color; A largely lacks these.
A shows extensive green or brown ground in true color, with vegetation often turning red in false color.
B shows snow filling openings and forming bands along terrain, interspersed with dark vegetation.

6.definition: A patch lies closer to A when exposed brown or tan soil occupies less of its area and leafy vegetation or open water occupies more. B is dominated by bare or sparsely vegetated agricultural fields.
cues: B has extensive brown–tan fields in true color, appearing cyan or muted gray-green in false color.
A generally has more green vegetation that becomes vivid red in false color.
B shows repeated narrow agricultural strips, with green or red vegetation confined to scattered strips and margins.
Continuous tree cover or open water favors A; water appears blue-green in true color and dark blue in false color.

7.definition: A patch lies closer to A when water has visible blue-green or gray reflectance and surface texture, or land forms open rectangular agricultural parcels. It lies closer to B when water is nearly black in both composites, or land has extensive dark-green woodland turning strongly red in false color. Use brightness together with spatial structure.
cues: Water: visible blue-green/gray tones and ripples toward A; nearly black, featureless surfaces toward B.
Land: straight boundaries and rectangular fields toward A; irregular, continuous wooded areas toward B.
Vegetation: varied green, muted red or pink parcels toward A; extensive vivid-red canopy toward B.

8.definition: A patch lies closer to A when more of its agricultural area consists of continuous green crop cover, appearing red or pink in false color. It lies closer to B when tan or pale brown fields dominate, appearing pale cyan or green in false color, with vegetation mainly in scattered trees or narrow corridors.
cues: A has extensive red or pink field interiors in false color; B has predominantly pale cyan or green fields.
True-color fields are frequently dark or vivid green in A, versus tan, straw-colored or light brown in B.
A's vegetation forms solid crop parcels; B's vegetation more often appears as isolated dots, clusters or streamside strips.
A generally has closely packed, narrow rectangular fields; B often has broader, less regular parcels.

9.definition: A patch lies closer to A when its farmland is dominated by fewer, wider, more expansive parcels. It lies closer to B when farmland is divided into many thin, elongated strips with closely spaced parallel boundaries. Judge parcel geometry across the patch rather than crop color.
cues: A has wider, blockier fields; B has more long, narrow ribbons.
B shows denser sequences of parallel field boundaries and alternating crop or soil bands.
A more often contains broad, uninterrupted field interiors with mottled texture.

10.definition: A patch lies closer to A when it shows relatively gentle terrain dominated by green vegetation, woodland or cultivated fields. It lies closer to B when pronounced ridges, shadowed valleys and brown or gray slopes dominate, often with scattered snow and less extensive vivid-red vegetation in false color.
cues: B has repeated ridges and deep terrain shadows; A generally lacks strong relief shading.
A has extensive green vegetation that turns red in false color; B has more brown, gray or muted vegetation cover.
Regular agricultural parcels support A; irregular slopes and branching valleys support B.
Scattered bright snow patches among exposed slopes support B; nearly complete white obscuration, as in A6, is inconclusive.

11.definition: A patch lies closer to A when broad, relatively uniform surfaces dominate, with fewer strong internal boundaries. It lies closer to B when contrasting surfaces form a dense mosaic of strips, blocks, or irregular fragments. Judge spatial texture and contrast across the whole patch.
cues: A has broad areas of nearly constant color; B has frequent abrupt changes in color or brightness.
B shows many distinct edges, including long field boundaries or intricate shorelines.
A is mostly continuous water, with one predominantly green landscape; B mixes dark surfaces with conspicuously lighter areas.
B’s agricultural patches alternate vegetated red strips with muted cyan or gray fields in false color.

12.definition: A patch lies closer to A when its background contains more pale or exposed surfaces—snow, tan agricultural soil, or light-colored water—and less dark water or dense green vegetation. Judge the underlying surface where visible; isolated bright clouds alone should not move a patch toward A.
cues: Extensive pale surfaces versus nearly black or dark-blue water in both composites.
Tan or pale agricultural fields versus predominantly green fields.
Broad white snow cover or uniformly pale water, rather than isolated white clouds.
More exposed ground and mixed field colors versus continuous vegetation that appears red in false color.

13.definition: A patch lies closer to A when its visible pattern breaks into smaller, more irregular elements with frequent local changes in brightness, color or texture. It lies closer to B when larger continuous areas dominate, with fewer internal interruptions. Compare spatial organization rather than land-cover identity.
cues: Fine mottling and frequent local transitions versus broad areas of similar appearance.
Small interwoven buildings, fields, vegetation or exposed ground versus larger coherent blocks.
Broken snow or shoreline patterns versus more continuous snow or vegetation cover.
Numerous irregular boundaries versus fewer long boundaries enclosing large parcels.

14.definition: A patch lies closer to A when its visible layout is dominated by long, straight, similarly oriented bands or boundaries. It lies closer to B when boundaries curve, change direction, or form a fragmented mosaic without one dominant orientation. Judge spatial organization rather than vegetation color or land-cover type.
cues: Long parallel edges or bands extending across much of the patch.
Elongated fields, planting rows, or woodland strips sharing a common orientation.
Straight, coherent major boundaries, including the shoreline in A5.
Toward B: irregular lake outlines, winding boundaries, and small parcels with varied orientations.

15.definition: A patch lies closer to A when light-toned, relatively uniform surfaces dominate, such as snow or exposed agricultural ground, often with bright red crop parcels in false color. It lies closer to B when dark water or rugged land with extensive dark slopes and shadows dominates. Judge the overall area and brightness of these surfaces.
cues: Large expanses of white or pale ground favor A; extensive deep blue, brown-black or black surfaces favor B.
Broad, bright red agricultural parcels in false color favor A; predominantly dark or muted false color favors B.
Regular field strips or continuous snow cover favor A.
Strongly shaded ridges and valleys, or dark water with fine ripple texture, favor B.

16.definition: A patch lies closer to A when it shows less visible ground snow or ice: predominantly vegetation, bare ground, or dark open water. B has extensive or patchy snow, appearing white in true color and bright cyan in false color, interspersed with darker terrain. Distinguish ground-following snow from clouds.
cues: White areas in true color that turn bright cyan in false color favor B.
Irregular snow patches tracing terrain and filling gaps among dark vegetation or rock favor B.
Green vegetation turning strongly red, including clear agricultural parcels, favors A.
Broad, uniformly dark water without bright snow or ice favors A.

17.definition: A patch lies closer to A if it shows exposed ground, buildings or vegetation rather than extensive bright snow cover. Green vegetation in true color and strong red vegetation in false color support A. Water-only patches are less diagnostic; these A examples look bluer and smoother than the darker, visibly rippled B examples.
cues: Extensive white cover across terrain, remaining white or pale cyan in false color, favors B.
Green vegetation that becomes vivid red in false color favors A.
Clearly exposed fields, streets and roofs with little white ground cover favor A.
For water-only scenes, blue and relatively smooth favors A; darker, more visibly rippled water favors B, weakly.

18.definition: A patch lies closer to A when it shows greener, snow-free land with stronger red vegetation in false color, or relatively bright green-blue water. B favors dark, sparsely vegetated fields, snow-like white/cyan cover, and very dark water. This describes visible appearance rather than establishing the season.
cues: Vegetation: extensive green land and strong false-color red favor A; subdued fields with isolated red strips favor B.
White cover with cyan detail in false color, as in B6, favors B.
Water: brighter green/teal in true color favors A; nearly black water in both composites favors B.
Water texture: smoother surfaces favor A; conspicuous repeated ripples favor B.

19.definition: A patch lies closer to A when more of its visible area consists of continuous dark blue water, with little near-infrared red response and few terrestrial features. It lies closer to B when vegetation, fields, roads, or other land textures occupy more of the scene. Featureless black areas alone are inconclusive.
cues: Extent of continuous dark blue water versus recognizable land cover.
Fine, repeated wave-like texture across broad areas at A.
Extensive red or pink vegetation in false color at B.
Field boundaries, roads, clearings, and varied terrestrial textures at B.
